subject: R^2 and ΔR^2 in a hierarchical regression

messages.author: bf07198e09758e0e
messages.subject: R^2 and ΔR^2 in a hierarchical regression
parts:
Hi everyone,

I'm using lavaan to conduct a hierarchical regression using latent variables, as I'm trying to follow best practices (e.g., as outlined in Westfall & Yarkoni, 2016). 

This is my first time using lavaan, and I would like to report R^2 and ΔR^2 for each step in the model, as would be reported in a hierarchical regression using observed variables. However, I am not sure where that information can be gleaned from. I know that you can request R^2 values with the command "summary(... rsquare = TRUE)", but that prints out individual r^2 values for each variable, rather than the multiple R^2 per each step. 

Is this something that can be done in lavaan?

Cheers,
Hayley

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: R^2 and ΔR^2 in a hierarchical regression
parts: I know that you can request R^2 values with the command "summary(... rsquare = TRUE)", but that prints out individual r^2 values for each variable, rather than the multiple R^2 per each step.

Well, R^2 is calculated for each outcome in a model, regardless of how many predictors it has.  So calculating ΔR^2 after adding more predictor(s) in a separate model is just a matter of subtracting the R^2 of the first model from the R^2 of the second model?  You can access those values in the parameterEstimates() function:

fit1 <- sem(...) # fewer predictors
fit2 <- sem(...) # more predictors, assuming the same outcomes
est1 <- parameterEstimates(fit1, rsquare = TRUE)
est2 <- parameterEstimates(fit2, rsquare = TRUE)
est2$est[est2$op == "r2"] - est1$est[est1$op == "r2"]

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

parts:
Hi Terrence, 

Thanks for your quick reply. That makes sense — my question was slightly different, but I think I've partly figured it out. I was confused that every single item, as well as manifest constructs, had a corresponding r^2 value. For example, I have a latent construct Cats that is manifested by Kitten 1, Kitten 2, and Kitten 3; and lavaan prints out a separate r^2 value next to each Kitten, often a very high value (e.g., .71). This didn't make sense to me because r^2 is the relative amount of variance of the dependent variable explained by the IVs, but the kittens are the just items that make up a construct. (I think that the answer may be something to do with the variance in participant responses and measurement error, but not 100% there).

In any case, I saw all of these values, and then arrived at the r^2 value for my key DV, and was unsure whether what I was looking at was related to the regression that I had requested from lavaan (i.e., the variance in the DV explained by my IVs) or some other mysterious value that related to the items used to create the manifest construct.

I now think that it actually *is* the regression equation, and I'm able to interpret the values that I see there. But this still leaves me a bit unsure about how the other regression coefficients are calculated. 

Any advice or links to relevant readings would be much appreciated.

Cheers,
Hayley

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: R^2 and ΔR^2 in a hierarchical regression
parts: This didn't make sense to me because r^2 is the relative amount of variance of the dependent variable explained by the IVs, but the kittens are the just items that make up a construct.

Factor loadings are regression slopes.  Indicators are DVs, and the latent construct is (hypothesized to be) their common cause ("common factor") that accounts for their covariance.  The R^2 for an indicator is the proportion of its variance that is explained by the common factor, and the remaining portion is due to item-specific uniqueness (including measurement error).
In any case, I saw all of these values, and then arrived at the r^2 value for my key DV,

The R^2 for your DV of interest (the common factor being predicted by other IVs) is the only value you need to pay attention to.  It has the same interpretation is R^2 always does, so you can probably follow whatever advice you were already following for calculating ΔR^2.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
